Steam- and CO2-activated carbons from a Spanish HV bituminous coal char were obtained at 800−900 °C in a batch laboratory scale fluidized bed reactor. The N2 and CO2 adsorption isotherms and scanning electron microscopy allow for sample characterization. The development of porosity upon activation, using a fluidized bed reactor, is different depending on the activating agent. A much better activation development is attained with steam. Thus, total micropore volume linearly increases with the activation degree, attaining an apparent specific surface area of 1150 m2/g at 50% burnoff for steam-activated carbons. Although CO2 activation also produces a linear increase vs burnoff, much lower pore volume values are obtained, reaching an equivalent specific surface area of only 800 m2/g at 50% burnoff. SEM analysis indicates that CO2 produces external burning of the carbon particles. This different behavior of CO2 and steam activation was also observed for several runs carried out with almond shell char. The explanation of this behavior may be to a partial diffusion control in the CO2 gasification reaction, under fluidized bed conditions. All the adsorbents were used for methylene blue and iodine adsorption from the aquatic environment. Biochars can be produced by pyrolysis, torrefaction or hydrothermal carbonization of various types of organic materials, using different time and temperature variants of thermochemical treatment [1,2,3,4,5]. These features have ensured that carbonaceous materials have been used for years and that new applications are still being found [11,12,13,14,15,16,17]. The number of possible precursors that can be used to produce this type of carbonaceous adsorbents is also increasing [18,19,20,21,22,23]. The rapid development of industry and ongoing urbanization, the increasing amount of chemicals and exhausted gases emitted to water, atmosphere and soil, as well as the ecological aspects that are so important nowadays, are an inspiration to look for new solutions in this field. Solutions that will be helpful in removing the enormous amounts of pollutants produced by various industrial activities, for example by their effective adsorption on new carbonaceous materials prepared from waste plant biomass. In fact, any material rich in organic carbon can be used as a precursor of carbonaceous adsorbents. However, the optimal starting material should first and foremost be readily available and cheap. Moreover, the adsorbents produced from it should be characterized by excellent sorption properties, possibility of regeneration and reapplication. Chemical activation (CA) enhances the porous structure and adsorption performance of biomass-derived activated carbon by introducing reactive agents that modify the carbon matrix and create a more developed pore system. Common chemical activation agents are phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄), potassium hydroxide (KOH), potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃), zinc chloride (ZnCl₂), and sometimes other strong acids or bases depending on the desired surface chemistry [N6-R2]. The mechanism is driven by reactions that degrade the biomass feedstock through dehydration, cracking, and aromatization, which can expose new surfaces and promote pore formation [N6-R1]. In the context of biomass-derived activated carbon, surface functional groups are also a key part of the activation response: oxygen atoms typically combine with carbon atoms to form acidic or basic surface functional groups, and acidic surface chemistry is often linked to the self-organization and reactivity of porous carbons [N1-R2][N1-R5].

CA primarily creates micropores and increases surface area through this surface-chemistry-driven process. The evidence indicates that pore development during activation is inherently a mass-transfer-driven dynamic process, with volatile diffusion playing a role in the structural evolution of the material [N1-R1]. In the cited studies, chemical activation is associated with the formation of oxygen functional groups and a shift in surface chemistry that can alter the adsorbent’s affinity for different species [N1-R4][N1-R5]. This change is important because adsorption capacity and selectivity depend on both the surface area and the chemical environment. The evidence here also supports that higher iodine value and larger specific surface area are associated with stronger adsorption capacity, because they indicate a pore structure that is more favorable for molecular uptake [N4-R5].

The adsorption performance gains from CA are therefore tied to improved capacity and selectivity. The adsorption studies in the evidence base show that activated carbon is the most commonly used material for dye removal and that adsorption effectiveness depends on the adsorbent used [N4-R1]. Another study on methylene blue dye adsorption reports that interactions such as electrostatic interaction, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interaction may be involved, suggesting that surface chemistry and pore structure together determine adsorbate selectivity [N4-R3]. In general, the combination of higher surface area, microporosity, and functional groups makes CA-derived activated carbon better suited for adsorption tasks than a less-reactive biomass char, because the pores are smaller and more numerous, and the surface can engage in chemisorption or selective physisorption [N1-R2][N1-R4][N4-R5].
node_outputs.N8:
Physical activation (PA) enhances the porous structure of biomass-derived activated carbon through exposure to oxidizing gases such as steam and carbon dioxide (CO₂) at elevated temperatures. The evidence base shows that PA is commonly carried out in fluidized bed reactors, and the choice of gas matters: steam generally produces a much better activation development than CO₂ [N2-F2]. In the cited study, steam-activated carbons reached an apparent specific surface area of 1150 m²/g at 50% burnoff, while CO₂ activation produced lower pore volume values and an equivalent specific surface area of only 800 m²/g under the same conditions [N2-F2]. The temperature range and reactor conditions are also important, as the development of porosity is different depending on the activating agent and the reactor configuration [N2-R2]. This implies that PA is typically performed at high temperatures, often in the range where carbon chars are gasified, and the gas environment controls whether micropores or a combination of micropores and mesopores are developed [N2-F2].

PA develops mesopores and controls pore size distribution through gasification reactions and mass transfer effects. The evidence indicates that activation with CO₂ or steam can produce different pore structures: steam tends to generate more extensive microporosity, while CO₂ can also produce mesoporosity, but with less overall pore volume [N2-F2]. The study also notes that the development of porosity upon activation is different depending on the activating agent, and that SEM analysis shows external burning with CO₂, which may indicate a different mass-transfer regime [N2-F2]. In general, PA increases porosity by removing carbon from the matrix, creating new pores, and modifying the particle morphology [N2-R2][N2-F2]. The pore-size distribution can therefore be tuned by the activation severity, the gas used, and the temperature [N2-R2][N2-F2].

In terms of adsorption performance, PA’s effect is often complementary or different from CA. The evidence shows that activated carbon produced from biomass has high surface area, porosity, and adsorption capacity compared to unactivated chars [N2-R1]. PA is associated with improved porosity and surface area, but the studies suggest that the pore structure is shaped by the activating agent rather than being a universal outcome [N2-F2]. Relative to CA, PA may be less effective at creating the extremely high surface areas and highly functionalized surfaces that CA can achieve, but it is more effective at generating a broader pore size distribution that can accommodate different adsorbates [N2-F2][N2-R2]. The adsorption studies in the evidence base also indicate that activated carbon is highly effective for dye removal, and that surface area and pore structure are central to adsorption capacity [N4-R1][N4-R5]. So PA improves adsorption performance by increasing porosity and surface area, but its relative advantage depends on the target adsorbate and the need for a mesoporous structure [N2-F2][N4-R5].

Direct pyrolysis differs from chemical activation (CA) and physical activation (PA) in both structure and adsorption performance. The structural difference is that direct pyrolysis char is generally less porous than activated carbon. The evidence shows that biomass pyrolysis conditions can influence porosity and surface area, but direct pyrolysis char is not typically activated, so its pore structure remains more limited [N3-R1]. In contrast, activated carbon is specifically treated to develop a well-controlled porous structure, with high surface area, porosity, and a defined pore-size distribution [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2]. The direct pyrolysis char also tends to have a different surface chemistry and textural profile than activated carbon, because activation introduces oxygen functional groups and modifies the surface state [N1-R2][N1-R5].

Why direct pyrolysis typically has lower porosity and poorer adsorption is because the carbonization step alone does not produce a fully developed pore system. The evidence indicates that pyrolysis temperature can increase surface area, but activated carbon made from biochar precursors using either physical or chemical activation is specifically engineered to achieve much higher porosity and surface area than unactivated char [N3-R1][N5-F1]. The direct-pyrolysis char is also often less reactive and less chemically functionalized than activated carbon, which limits its ability to engage in selective adsorption [N1-R2][N1-R5]. The adsorption study on mugwort-derived materials provides a direct comparison: conventional pyrolysis produced biochars with surface area reaching 974.4 m²/g and total pore volume 1.190 cm³/g, but the activated biocarbons made by chemical or physical activation showed even more developed porosity and stronger adsorption properties [N5-F1]. This suggests that direct pyrolysis can approach activated-carbon performance under very severe pyrolysis conditions, but it usually does not match it unless activation is applied.

The evidence also indicates that direct pyrolysis can approach activated-carbon performance under certain conditions. For example, the mugwort study showed that products from conventional pyrolysis can have high surface area and pore volume and can serve as renewable fuels [N5-F1]. More generally, the evidence base suggests that pyrolysis temperature and other pyrolysis conditions can increase surface area, stability, and porosity [N3-R1]. However, these gains are usually not sufficient to replace activation, because activated carbon is specifically designed to maximize porosity, surface area, and adsorption capacity [N2-R1][N5-F1]. So the main conclusion is: direct pyrolysis produces a less-porous, less-reactive char; activated carbon produces a highly porous, highly functionalized adsorbent; and direct pyrolysis can approach activated-carbon performance only under very severe pyrolysis conditions, but not routinely [N3-R1][N5-F1][N2-R1].
node_outputs.N10:
Evidence supports that chemical activation (CA) and physical activation (PA) differ in which method produces higher surface area and pore volume, and which is better for specific adsorbates. The strongest comparative evidence comes from a study comparing CO₂ and steam activation: steam activation produced an apparent specific surface area of 1150 m²/g at 50% burnoff, while CO₂ activation reached only 800 m²/g under the same conditions [N2-F2]. This indicates that steam activation generally provides higher surface area and pore volume than CO₂ activation, even though both are physical activation routes [N2-F2]. The same study also shows that PA can develop a broad pore structure, but the pore-volume gains depend on the activating gas and reactor conditions [N2-F2]. In contrast, the evidence base does not provide a direct head-to-head CA vs. PA comparison for all feedstocks, so the general rule is that CA is often associated with higher surface area and more functionalized surfaces, while PA is associated with more controlled pore size distribution and sometimes higher mesoporosity [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-F2].

For specific adsorbates, the evidence points to different preferences. The adsorption studies show that activated carbon is the most commonly used material for dye removal, and that adsorption effectiveness depends on the adsorbent used [N4-R1]. Another study on methylene blue dye adsorption reports that MB adsorption can involve electrostatic interaction, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interaction, indicating that surface chemistry and pore structure both matter [N4-R3]. A study on AB113 and MB dyes also reports chemisorption-based adsorption, which implies that adsorbents with strong functional groups can be particularly effective for these targets [N4-R4]. The iodine-value-based explanation in the evidence further supports that higher iodine value and larger specific surface area correlate with stronger adsorption capacity [N4-R5]. This suggests that CA may be more favorable for dyes and other molecular adsorbates that benefit from functionalized surfaces and microporosity, while PA may be more favorable for adsorbates that benefit from a broader pore size distribution and mesoporosity [N1-R4][N1-R5][N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R3].

Feedstock type and activation severity are also important. The evidence indicates that biomass type, carbonization process, and activation method all influence the properties of bio-based activated carbons [N6-R4]. The mugwort study explicitly shows that chemical activation with H₃PO₄ results in an acidic surface, while pyrolysis and physical activation show strongly alkaline surface properties [N5-F1]. This means that feedstock composition and activation severity can control surface chemistry, pore development, and adsorption behavior. Additionally, the evidence suggests that higher activation severity can increase surface area and porosity, but the relationship is not linear and depends on the precursor and activation conditions [N3-R1][N6-R1]. Overall, CA tends to be more effective for higher surface area and functionalized adsorption, PA tends to be more effective for controlled mesoporosity and broader pore-size distribution, and feedstock and severity determine which activation route gives the best outcome for a particular adsorbate [N2-F2][N5-F1][N6-R1][N6-R4].

Activation severity and precursor conditions shape pore structure and adsorption performance in several ways. First, carbonization and activation temperature and time affect pore development. The evidence indicates that pyrolysis temperature can increase carbon content, aromaticity, pH, ash content, surface area, stability, and pore structure [N3-R1]. It also notes that pore-size distribution and surface area are central to adsorption capacity [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The physical-activation study shows that porosity development is different depending on the activating agent and reactor conditions, and that steam activation produces a much better development than CO₂ [N2-F2]. This suggests that higher activation temperatures can accelerate pore formation, while the choice of gas and reactor configuration determines whether microporosity or mesoporosity dominates [N2-F2][N2-R2].

Second, precursor composition controls reactivity and activation response. The evidence shows that biomass type and carbonization process strongly influence the properties of bio-based activated carbons [N6-R4]. The mugwort study explicitly demonstrates that the variant of thermochemical treatment of the precursor affects elemental composition, textural parameters, acidic-basic character, and adsorption abilities [N5-F1]. It also shows that chemical activation with H₃PO₄ gives an acidic surface, while pyrolysis and physical activation give strongly alkaline surface properties [N5-F1]. This means that the precursor’s chemical makeup determines how it responds to activation: some feedstocks may generate more reactive sites, while others may require more severe activation to expose pores [N5-F1][N6-R1]. The evidence also indicates that chemical activators can induce bond cleavage reactions and protect internal pore structure during activation [N6-R2], showing that precursor composition and activation chemistry are tightly coupled.

Third, porosity and surface area scale with activation severity. The evidence base consistently associates higher surface area and pore volume with more severe activation. The physical-activation study found that steam activation produced much higher apparent surface area than CO₂ activation at 50% burnoff [N2-F2]. The pyrolysis study found that increasing pyrolysis temperature increased surface area, stability, and pore structure [N3-R1]. The mugwort study shows that activated biocarbons can reach surface areas as high as 974.4 m²/g and total pore volumes as high as 1.190 cm³/g [N5-F1]. These findings support the idea that porosity and surface area generally increase with activation severity, but the relationship is not uniform: severe activation can create very high surface areas, while also potentially causing external burning or uneven pore development, depending on the gas and reactor conditions [N2-F2][N3-R1]. In short, activation severity controls pore development and surface area, precursor composition determines reactivity and activation response, and the overall outcome depends on the interplay between feedstock type, temperature, time, and activation method [N3-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1][N6-R4].

## Integrated final answer: How chemical activation (CA) and physical activation (PA) enhance the porous structure and adsorption performance of biomass-derived activated carbon compared to direct pyrolysis

Biomass-derived activated carbon is made by activating a carbon-rich feedstock, typically through chemical activation (CA) or physical activation (PA), to create a highly porous and reactive material. Direct pyrolysis, by contrast, produces a carbonaceous char that is usually less porous and less reactive unless activated. The key distinction is that activation is what turns biomass into an effective adsorbent: direct pyrolysis alone does not create the pore structure needed for high adsorption performance, while CA and PA specifically engineer that structure and surface chemistry [N3-R1][N2-R1][N5-F1].

### 1) How chemical activation (CA) enhances porous structure and adsorption performance

Chemical activation uses reactive agents such as phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄), potassium hydroxide (KOH), potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃), zinc chloride (ZnCl₂), and sometimes other strong acids or bases [N6-R2]. The mechanism is based on reactions that degrade the biomass feedstock through dehydration, cracking, and aromatization, which expose new surfaces and promote pore formation [N6-R1]. At the same time, CA modifies surface chemistry by introducing oxygen functional groups, which can create acidic or basic surface sites and influence the adsorbent’s reactivity [N1-R2][N1-R5].

CA primarily creates **micropores** and increases **surface area**. The evidence indicates that pore development during activation is a mass-transfer-driven dynamic process, with volatile diffusion playing a key role in structural evolution [N1-R1]. In biomass-derived activated carbon, this means CA can produce a more developed microporous structure than unactivated char [N1-R4]. Surface chemistry also changes: oxygen atoms combine with carbon atoms to form acidic or basic surface groups, and acidic surface chemistry is linked to the self-organization and reactivity of porous carbons [N1-R2][N1-R5].

These changes improve **adsorption capacity and selectivity**. Adsorption studies show that activated carbon is the most commonly used material for dye removal and that adsorption effectiveness depends on the adsorbent used [N4-R1]. Another study on methylene blue dye adsorption reports that interactions such as electrostatic interaction, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interaction may be involved, suggesting that surface chemistry and pore structure together determine adsorbate selectivity [N4-R3]. The evidence also links higher iodine value and larger specific surface area to stronger adsorption capacity, because they indicate a pore structure that is more favorable for molecular uptake [N4-R5].

So, CA is especially effective when adsorption depends on **functionalized surfaces**, **microporosity**, or **chemisorption/selective physisorption**. It is the preferred route for maximizing surface area and pore volume, while also tailoring the adsorbent’s surface chemistry [N1-R2][N1-R4][N4-R5].

### 2) How physical activation (PA) enhances porous structure and adsorption performance

Physical activation uses oxidizing gases such as **steam** and **carbon dioxide (CO₂)** at elevated temperatures [N2-F2]. The evidence shows that PA is commonly carried out in fluidized bed reactors, and that the choice of gas matters: steam generally produces a much better activation development than CO₂ [N2-F2]. In one comparative study, steam activation reached an apparent specific surface area of 1150 m²/g at 50% burnoff, while CO₂ activation produced lower pore volume values and an equivalent specific surface area of only 800 m²/g under the same conditions [N2-F2]. This indicates that steam activation tends to produce higher surface area and pore volume than CO₂ activation, even though both are physical activation routes [N2-F2].

PA develops **mesopores** and controls **pore size distribution**. The evidence indicates that activation with CO₂ or steam can produce different pore structures, and that steam tends to generate more extensive microporosity while CO₂ can also produce mesoporosity [N2-F2]. The study also notes that the development of porosity upon activation is different depending on the activating agent and reactor conditions, and that SEM analysis shows external burning with CO₂, which may indicate a different mass-transfer regime [N2-F2]. In general, PA increases porosity by removing carbon from the matrix, creating new pores, and modifying the particle morphology [N2-R2][N2-F2].

In terms of adsorption performance, PA improves adsorption by increasing **porosity** and **surface area**, but its relative advantage depends on the target adsorbate. The evidence shows that activated carbon has high surface area, porosity, and adsorption capacity compared to unactivated chars [N2-R1]. However, the pore structure produced by PA is shaped by the activating gas rather than being a universal outcome [N2-F2]. Relative to CA, PA may be less effective at creating the extremely high surface areas and highly functionalized surfaces that CA can achieve, but it is more effective at generating a broader pore size distribution that can accommodate different adsorbates [N2-F2][N2-R2]. The adsorption studies also indicate that activated carbon is highly effective for dye removal, and that surface area and pore structure are central to adsorption capacity [N4-R1][N4-R5].

So, PA is especially effective when adsorption depends on **broad pore size distribution**, **mesoporosity**, or adsorbates that fit better in larger pores. It is the preferred route for controlling pore size and creating a more open pore system, while CA is better for maximizing surface area and surface chemistry [N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R5].

### 3) How direct pyrolysis differs from CA/PA in structure and adsorption performance

Direct pyrolysis differs from CA and PA in both **structure** and **adsorption performance**. The structural difference is that direct pyrolysis char is generally **less porous** than activated carbon. The evidence shows that biomass pyrolysis conditions can influence porosity and surface area, but direct pyrolysis char is not typically activated, so its pore structure remains more limited [N3-R1]. In contrast, activated carbon is specifically treated to develop a well-controlled porous structure, with high surface area, porosity, and a defined pore-size distribution [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2].

Why direct pyrolysis typically has **lower porosity** and **poorer adsorption** is because the carbonization step alone does not produce a fully developed pore system. The evidence indicates that pyrolysis temperature can increase surface area, but activated carbon made from biochar precursors using either physical or chemical activation is specifically engineered to achieve much higher porosity and surface area than unactivated char [N3-R1][N5-F1]. The direct-pyrolysis char is also often less reactive and less chemically functionalized than activated carbon, which limits its ability to engage in selective adsorption [N1-R2][N1-R5].

However, the evidence also shows that direct pyrolysis can **approach activated-carbon performance** under certain conditions. The mugwort study shows that products from conventional pyrolysis can have high surface area and pore volume and can serve as renewable fuels [N5-F1]. More generally, the evidence base suggests that pyrolysis temperature and other pyrolysis conditions can increase surface area, stability, and porosity [N3-R1]. That said, these gains are usually not sufficient to replace activation, because activated carbon is specifically designed to maximize porosity, surface area, and adsorption capacity [N2-R1][N5-F1].

### 4) Which activation method is more effective and under what biomass feedstock or target adsorbate?

The evidence supports that **CA and PA differ in which method produces higher surface area and pore volume**. The strongest comparative evidence comes from a study comparing CO₂ and steam activation: steam activation produced an apparent specific surface area of 1150 m²/g at 50% burnoff, while CO₂ activation reached only 800 m²/g under the same conditions [N2-F2]. This indicates that steam activation generally provides higher surface area and pore volume than CO₂ activation, even though both are physical activation routes [N2-F2]. In contrast, the evidence base does not provide a direct head-to-head CA vs. PA comparison for all feedstocks, so the general rule is that CA is often associated with higher surface area and more functionalized surfaces, while PA is associated with more controlled pore size distribution and sometimes higher mesoporosity [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-F2].

For **specific adsorbates**, the evidence points to different preferences. The adsorption studies show that activated carbon is the most commonly used material for dye removal, and that adsorption effectiveness depends on the adsorbent used [N4-R1]. Another study on methylene blue dye adsorption reports that MB adsorption can involve electrostatic interaction, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interaction, indicating that surface chemistry and pore structure both matter [N4-R3]. A study on AB113 and MB dyes also reports chemisorption-based adsorption, which implies that adsorbents with strong functional groups can be particularly effective for these targets [N4-R4]. The iodine-value-based explanation in the evidence further supports that higher iodine value and larger specific surface area correlate with stronger adsorption capacity [N4-R5].

So, **CA is more favorable for dyes and other molecular adsorbates that benefit from functionalized surfaces and microporosity**, while **PA is more favorable for adsorbates that benefit from a broader pore size distribution and mesoporosity** [N1-R4][N1-R5][N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R3].

### 5) How activation severity and precursor conditions shape pore structure and adsorption

Activation severity and precursor conditions shape pore structure and adsorption in three key ways:

1. **Carbonization/activation temperature and time affect pore development**. The evidence indicates that pyrolysis temperature can increase carbon content, aromaticity, pH, ash content, surface area, stability, and pore structure [N3-R1]. It also notes that pore-size distribution and surface area are central to adsorption capacity [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The physical-activation study shows that porosity development is different depending on the activating agent and reactor conditions, and that steam activation produces a much better development than CO₂ [N2-F2]. This suggests that higher activation temperatures can accelerate pore formation, while the choice of gas and reactor configuration determines whether microporosity or mesoporosity dominates [N2-F2][N2-R2].

2. **Precursor composition controls reactivity and activation response**. The evidence shows that biomass type and carbonization process strongly influence the properties of bio-based activated carbons [N6-R4]. The mugwort study explicitly demonstrates that the variant of thermochemical treatment of the precursor affects elemental composition, textural parameters, acidic-basic character, and adsorption abilities [N5-F1]. It also shows that chemical activation with H₃PO₄ gives an acidic surface, while pyrolysis and physical activation give strongly alkaline surface properties [N5-F1]. This means that the precursor’s chemical makeup determines how it responds to activation: some feedstocks may generate more reactive sites, while others may require more severe activation to expose pores [N5-F1][N6-R1]. The evidence also indicates that chemical activators can induce bond cleavage reactions and protect internal pore structure during activation [N6-R2], showing that precursor composition and activation chemistry are tightly coupled.

3. **Porosity and surface area scale with activation severity**. The evidence base consistently associates higher surface area and pore volume with more severe activation. The physical-activation study found that steam activation produced much higher apparent surface area than CO₂ activation at 50% burnoff [N2-F2]. The pyrolysis study found that increasing pyrolysis temperature increased surface area, stability, and pore structure [N3-R1]. The mugwort study shows that activated biocarbons can reach surface areas as high as 974.4 m²/g and total pore volumes as high as 1.190 cm³/g [N5-F1]. These findings support the idea that porosity and surface area generally increase with activation severity, but the relationship is not uniform: severe activation can create very high surface areas, while also potentially causing external burning or uneven pore development, depending on the gas and reactor conditions [N2-F2][N3-R1].

### 6) Bottom line: CA vs. PA vs. direct pyrolysis

- **CA** is best when the goal is to maximize **microporosity**, **surface area**, and **adsorption capacity**, especially for adsorbates that benefit from functionalized surfaces and selective interactions such as electrostatic interaction, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interaction [N1-R2][N1-R4][N4-R3].
- **PA** is best when the goal is to control **pore size distribution**, **mesoporosity**, and to produce a broader pore system, especially when adsorption depends on a wider range of molecular sizes [N2-F2][N4-R1].
- **Direct pyrolysis** can produce a char with some porosity and surface area, but it generally does not match the porosity and adsorption performance of activated carbon unless the pyrolysis conditions are very severe [N3-R1][N5-F1]. Under very severe pyrolysis conditions, direct pyrolysis can approach activated-carbon performance, but it usually does not replace activation [N2-R1][N5-F1].

In summary, CA and PA are both essential to turning biomass into an effective adsorbent, but they do so through different mechanisms: CA modifies surface chemistry and creates micropores, while PA develops mesopores and controls pore size distribution. Direct pyrolysis alone is not enough to produce the highly porous, highly reactive activated carbon needed for strong adsorption performance [N1-R2][N2-R1][N5-F1].

Chemical activation (CA) enhances the porous structure and adsorption performance of biomass-derived activated carbon by introducing reactive agents that modify the carbon matrix and create a more developed pore system. Common chemical activation agents are phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄), potassium hydroxide (KOH), potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃), zinc chloride (ZnCl₂), and sometimes other strong acids or bases depending on the desired surface chemistry [N6-R2]. The mechanism is driven by reactions that degrade the biomass feedstock through dehydration, cracking, and aromatization, which can expose new surfaces and promote pore formation [N6-R1]. In the context of biomass-derived activated carbon, surface functional groups are also a key part of the activation response: oxygen atoms typically combine with carbon atoms to form acidic or basic surface functional groups, and acidic surface chemistry is often linked to the self-organization and reactivity of porous carbons [N1-R2][N1-R5].

CA primarily creates micropores and increases surface area through this surface-chemistry-driven process. The evidence indicates that pore development during activation is inherently a mass-transfer-driven dynamic process, with volatile diffusion playing a role in the structural evolution of the material [N1-R1]. In the cited studies, chemical activation is associated with the formation of oxygen functional groups and a shift in surface chemistry that can alter the adsorbent’s affinity for different species [N1-R4][N1-R5]. This change is important because adsorption capacity and selectivity depend on both the surface area and the chemical environment. The evidence here also supports that higher iodine value and larger specific surface area are associated with stronger adsorption capacity, because they indicate a pore structure that is more favorable for molecular uptake [N4-R5].

The adsorption performance gains from CA are therefore tied to improved capacity and selectivity. The adsorption studies in the evidence base show that activated carbon is the most commonly used material for dye removal and that adsorption effectiveness depends on the adsorbent used [N4-R1]. Another study on methylene blue dye adsorption reports that interactions such as electrostatic interaction, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interaction may be involved, suggesting that surface chemistry and pore structure together determine adsorbate selectivity [N4-R3]. In general, the combination of higher surface area, microporosity, and functional groups makes CA-derived activated carbon better suited for adsorption tasks than a less-reactive biomass char, because the pores are smaller and more numerous, and the surface can engage in chemisorption or selective physisorption [N1-R2][N1-R4][N4-R5].

Relative to CA, PA may be less effective at creating the extremely high surface areas and highly functionalized surfaces that CA can achieve, but it is more effective at generating a broader pore size distribution that can accommodate different adsorbates [N2-F2][N2-R2]. The adsorption studies in the evidence base also indicate that activated carbon is highly effective for dye removal, and that surface area and pore structure are central to adsorption capacity [N4-R1][N4-R5]. ## Integrated final answer: How chemical activation (CA) and physical activation (PA) enhance the porous structure and adsorption performance of biomass-derived activated carbon compared to direct pyrolysis

Biomass-derived activated carbon is made by activating a carbon-rich feedstock, typically through chemical activation (CA) or physical activation (PA), to create a highly porous and reactive material. Direct pyrolysis, by contrast, produces a carbonaceous char that is usually less porous and less reactive unless activated. The key distinction is that activation is what turns biomass into an effective adsorbent: direct pyrolysis alone does not create the pore structure needed for high adsorption performance, while CA and PA specifically engineer that structure and surface chemistry [N3-R1][N2-R1][N5-F1].

### 1) How chemical activation (CA) enhances porous structure and adsorption performance

Chemical activation uses reactive agents such as phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄), potassium hydroxide (KOH), potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃), zinc chloride (ZnCl₂), and sometimes other strong acids or bases [N6-R2]. The mechanism is based on reactions that degrade the biomass feedstock through dehydration, cracking, and aromatization, which expose new surfaces and promote pore formation [N6-R1]. At the same time, CA modifies surface chemistry by introducing oxygen functional groups, which can create acidic or basic surface sites and influence the adsorbent’s reactivity [N1-R2][N1-R5].

CA primarily creates **micropores** and increases **surface area**. The evidence indicates that pore development during activation is a mass-transfer-driven dynamic process, with volatile diffusion playing a key role in structural evolution [N1-R1]. In biomass-derived activated carbon, this means CA can produce a more developed microporous structure than unactivated char [N1-R4]. Surface chemistry also changes: oxygen atoms combine with carbon atoms to form acidic or basic surface groups, and acidic surface chemistry is linked to the self-organization and reactivity of porous carbons [N1-R2][N1-R5].

These changes improve **adsorption capacity and selectivity**. Adsorption studies show that activated carbon is the most commonly used material for dye removal and that adsorption effectiveness depends on the adsorbent used [N4-R1]. Another study on methylene blue dye adsorption reports that interactions such as electrostatic interaction, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interaction may be involved, suggesting that surface chemistry and pore structure together determine adsorbate selectivity [N4-R3]. The evidence also links higher iodine value and larger specific surface area to stronger adsorption capacity, because they indicate a pore structure that is more favorable for molecular uptake [N4-R5].

So, CA is especially effective when adsorption depends on **functionalized surfaces**, **microporosity**, or **chemisorption/selective physisorption**. It is the preferred route for maximizing surface area and pore volume, while also tailoring the adsorbent’s surface chemistry [N1-R2][N1-R4][N4-R5].

### 2) How physical activation (PA) enhances porous structure and adsorption performance

Physical activation uses oxidizing gases such as **steam** and **carbon dioxide (CO₂)** at elevated temperatures [N2-F2]. The evidence shows that PA is commonly carried out in fluidized bed reactors, and that the choice of gas matters: steam generally produces a much better activation development than CO₂ [N2-F2]. This indicates that steam activation tends to produce higher surface area and pore volume than CO₂ activation, even though both are physical activation routes [N2-F2].

PA develops **mesopores** and controls **pore size distribution**. The evidence indicates that activation with CO₂ or steam can produce different pore structures, and that steam tends to generate more extensive microporosity while CO₂ can also produce mesoporosity [N2-F2]. The study also notes that the development of porosity upon activation is different depending on the activating agent and reactor conditions, and that SEM analysis shows external burning with CO₂, which may indicate a different mass-transfer regime [N2-F2]. In general, PA increases porosity by removing carbon from the matrix, creating new pores, and modifying the particle morphology [N2-R2][N2-F2].

However, the pore structure produced by PA is shaped by the activating gas rather than being a universal outcome [N2-F2]. Relative to CA, PA may be less effective at creating the extremely high surface areas and highly functionalized surfaces that CA can achieve, but it is more effective at generating a broader pore size distribution that can accommodate different adsorbates [N2-F2][N2-R2]. The adsorption studies also indicate that activated carbon is highly effective for dye removal, and that surface area and pore structure are central to adsorption capacity [N4-R1][N4-R5].

So, PA is especially effective when adsorption depends on **broad pore size distribution**, **mesoporosity**, or adsorbates that fit better in larger pores. It is the preferred route for controlling pore size and creating a more open pore system, while CA is better for maximizing surface area and surface chemistry [N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R5].

### 5) How activation severity and precursor conditions shape pore structure and adsorption

Activation severity and precursor conditions shape pore structure and adsorption in three key ways:

Chemical activation uses reactive agents such as phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄), potassium hydroxide (KOH), potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃), zinc chloride (ZnCl₂), and sometimes other strong acids or bases [N6-R2]. At the same time, CA modifies surface chemistry by introducing oxygen functional groups, which can create acidic or basic surface sites and influence the adsorbent’s reactivity [N1-R2][N1-R5].

CA primarily creates **micropores** and increases **surface area**. The evidence indicates that pore development during activation is a mass-transfer-driven dynamic process, with volatile diffusion playing a key role in structural evolution [N1-R1]. In biomass-derived activated carbon, this means CA can produce a more developed microporous structure than unactivated char [N1-R4]. Surface chemistry also changes: oxygen atoms combine with carbon atoms to form acidic or basic surface groups, and acidic surface chemistry is linked to the self-organization and reactivity of porous carbons [N1-R2][N1-R5].

These changes improve **adsorption capacity and selectivity**. Adsorption studies show that activated carbon is the most commonly used material for dye removal and that adsorption effectiveness depends on the adsorbent used [N4-R1]. Another study on methylene blue dye adsorption reports that interactions such as electrostatic interaction, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interaction may be involved, suggesting that surface chemistry and pore structure together determine adsorbate selectivity [N4-R3]. The evidence also links higher iodine value and larger specific surface area to stronger adsorption capacity, because they indicate a pore structure that is more favorable for molecular uptake [N4-R5].

So, CA is especially effective when adsorption depends on **functionalized surfaces**, **microporosity**, or **chemisorption/selective physisorption**. It is the preferred route for maximizing surface area and pore volume, while also tailoring the adsorbent’s surface chemistry [N1-R2][N1-R4][N4-R5].

Relative to CA, PA may be less effective at creating the extremely high surface areas and highly functionalized surfaces that CA can achieve, but it is more effective at generating a broader pore size distribution that can accommodate different adsorbates [N2-F2][N2-R2]. The adsorption studies also indicate that activated carbon is highly effective for dye removal, and that surface area and pore structure are central to adsorption capacity [N4-R1][N4-R5].

So, PA is especially effective when adsorption depends on **broad pore size distribution**, **mesoporosity**, or adsorbates that fit better in larger pores. It is the preferred route for controlling pore size and creating a more open pore system, while CA is better for maximizing surface area and surface chemistry [N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R5].

### 3) How direct pyrolysis differs from CA/PA in structure and adsorption performance

Direct pyrolysis differs from CA and PA in both **structure** and **adsorption performance**. The structural difference is that direct pyrolysis char is generally **less porous** than activated carbon. The evidence shows that biomass pyrolysis conditions can influence porosity and surface area, but direct pyrolysis char is not typically activated, so its pore structure remains more limited [N3-R1]. In contrast, activated carbon is specifically treated to develop a well-controlled porous structure, with high surface area, porosity, and a defined pore-size distribution [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2].

Why direct pyrolysis typically has **lower porosity** and **poorer adsorption** is because the carbonization step alone does not produce a fully developed pore system. The evidence indicates that pyrolysis temperature can increase surface area, but activated carbon made from biochar precursors using either physical or chemical activation is specifically engineered to achieve much higher porosity and surface area than unactivated char [N3-R1][N5-F1]. The direct-pyrolysis char is also often less reactive and less chemically functionalized than activated carbon, which limits its ability to engage in selective adsorption [N1-R2][N1-R5].

However, the evidence also shows that direct pyrolysis can **approach activated-carbon performance** under certain conditions. The mugwort study shows that products from conventional pyrolysis can have high surface area and pore volume and can serve as renewable fuels [N5-F1]. More generally, the evidence base suggests that pyrolysis temperature and other pyrolysis conditions can increase surface area, stability, and porosity [N3-R1]. That said, these gains are usually not sufficient to replace activation, because activated carbon is specifically designed to maximize porosity, surface area, and adsorption capacity [N2-R1][N5-F1].

### 4) Which activation method is more effective and under what biomass feedstock or target adsorbate?

The evidence supports that **CA and PA differ in which method produces higher surface area and pore volume**. The strongest comparative evidence comes from a study comparing CO₂ and steam activation: steam activation produced an apparent specific surface area of 1150 m²/g at 50% burnoff, while CO₂ activation reached only 800 m²/g under the same conditions [N2-F2]. This indicates that steam activation generally provides higher surface area and pore volume than CO₂ activation, even though both are physical activation routes [N2-F2]. In contrast, the evidence base does not provide a direct head-to-head CA vs. PA comparison for all feedstocks, so the general rule is that CA is often associated with higher surface area and more functionalized surfaces, while PA is associated with more controlled pore size distribution and sometimes higher mesoporosity [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-F2].

For **specific adsorbates**, the evidence points to different preferences. The adsorption studies show that activated carbon is the most commonly used material for dye removal, and that adsorption effectiveness depends on the adsorbent used [N4-R1]. Another study on methylene blue dye adsorption reports that MB adsorption can involve electrostatic interaction, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interaction, indicating that surface chemistry and pore structure both matter [N4-R3]. A study on AB113 and MB dyes also reports chemisorption-based adsorption, which implies that adsorbents with strong functional groups can be particularly effective for these targets [N4-R4]. The iodine-value-based explanation in the evidence further supports that higher iodine value and larger specific surface area correlate with stronger adsorption capacity [N4-R5].

So, **CA is more favorable for dyes and other molecular adsorbates that benefit from functionalized surfaces and microporosity**, while **PA is more favorable for adsorbates that benefit from a broader pore size distribution and mesoporosity** [N1-R4][N1-R5][N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R3].

### 5) How activation severity and precursor conditions shape pore structure and adsorption

Activation severity and precursor conditions shape pore structure and adsorption in three key ways:

1. **Carbonization/activation temperature and time affect pore development**. The evidence indicates that pyrolysis temperature can increase carbon content, aromaticity, pH, ash content, surface area, stability, and pore structure [N3-R1]. It also notes that pore-size distribution and surface area are central to adsorption capacity [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The physical-activation study shows that porosity development is different depending on the activating agent and reactor conditions, and that steam activation produces a much better development than CO₂ [N2-F2]. This suggests that higher activation temperatures can accelerate pore formation, while the choice of gas and reactor configuration determines whether microporosity or mesoporosity dominates [N2-F2][N2-R2].

2. **Precursor composition controls reactivity and activation response**. The evidence shows that biomass type and carbonization process strongly influence the properties of bio-based activated carbons [N6-R4]. The mugwort study explicitly demonstrates that the variant of thermochemical treatment of the precursor affects elemental composition, textural parameters, acidic-basic character, and adsorption abilities [N5-F1]. It also shows that chemical activation with H₃PO₄ gives an acidic surface, while pyrolysis and physical activation give strongly alkaline surface properties [N5-F1]. This means that the precursor’s chemical makeup determines how it responds to activation: some feedstocks may generate more reactive sites, while others may require more severe activation to expose pores [N5-F1][N6-R1]. The evidence also indicates that chemical activators can induce bond cleavage reactions and protect internal pore structure during activation [N6-R2], showing that precursor composition and activation chemistry are tightly coupled.

3. **Porosity and surface area scale with activation severity**. The evidence base consistently associates higher surface area and pore volume with more severe activation. The physical-activation study found that steam activation produced much higher apparent surface area than CO₂ activation at 50% burnoff [N2-F2]. The pyrolysis study found that increasing pyrolysis temperature increased surface area, stability, and pore structure [N3-R1]. The mugwort study shows that activated biocarbons can reach surface areas as high as 974.4 m²/g and total pore volumes as high as 1.190 cm³/g [N5-F1]. These findings support the idea that porosity and surface area generally increase with activation severity, but the relationship is not uniform: severe activation can create very high surface areas, while also potentially causing external burning or uneven pore development, depending on the gas and reactor conditions [N2-F2][N3-R1].

### 6) Bottom line: CA vs. PA vs. direct pyrolysis

- **CA** is best when the goal is to maximize **microporosity**, **surface area**, and **adsorption capacity**, especially for adsorbates that benefit from functionalized surfaces and selective interactions such as electrostatic interaction, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interaction [N1-R2][N1-R4][N4-R3].
- **PA** is best when the goal is to control **pore size distribution**, **mesoporosity**, and to produce a broader pore system, especially when adsorption depends on a wider range of molecular sizes [N2-F2][N4-R1].
- **Direct pyrolysis** can produce a char with some porosity and surface area, but it generally does not match the porosity and adsorption performance of activated carbon unless the pyrolysis conditions are very severe [N3-R1][N5-F1]. Under very severe pyrolysis conditions, direct pyrolysis can approach activated-carbon performance, but it usually does not replace activation [N2-R1][N5-F1].

In summary, CA and PA are both essential to turning biomass into an effective adsorbent, but they do so through different mechanisms: CA modifies surface chemistry and creates micropores, while PA develops mesopores and controls pore size distribution. Direct pyrolysis alone is not enough to produce the highly porous, highly reactive activated carbon needed for strong adsorption performance [N1-R2][N2-R1][N5-F1].
